item.title: GTA 6 is locked to 30fps on my PS5, but I found a way to play it at 60fps through my PC
item.itunes:title: GTA 6 is locked to 30fps on my PS5, but I found a way to play it at 60fps through my PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A day before the highly anticipated launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar Games told Kotaku that even the PS5 Pro lacked the CPU headroom to run the game at 60fps, and that no 40fps or 60fps mode would come to current-gen consoles. Some players, myself included, thought differently.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I decided the game wasn't worth playing at a locked 30fps, so I stayed up all Friday night streaming it from my PS5 to my PC. Using a capture card was the most popular trick, but I thought that an $80 game shouldn't need a $160 device to run at the frame rate I wanted.

Sony's Remote Play app was an embarrassment that kept crashing, my controller kept kicking me out of the stream, and the first frame generation setup made driving feel like driving a bad RC car. After hours of work, I finally found a free, open-source tool that looks and feels like the performance mode Rockstar never shipped.

Leonida deserves more than 30 frames a second

And my base PS5 can't always give me that

GTA 6 is perhaps the most ambitious, visually rich, and densely simulated game of the decade. Leonida is bursting with detail, its streets teeming with life, and there are an impossible number of things happening on screen no matter where you find yourself in the world. Even on the base PS5, it renders at 1440p with ray-traced reflections and global illumination, but ironically, everything in the game environment tells you this is a world meant to be moved through fluidly, and a locked 30fps does a disservice to all of it.

What makes it worse is that 30fps is a ceiling, not a floor, on my console. In its launch week, Digital Foundry caught the base PS5 slipping below 30fps when driving hard, and dropping to the mid-20s for entire stretches once explosions started piling up. The reviewers added that the PS5 Pro seemed to fare much better in the same tests, but perhaps that's what Sony's marketing around "PS5 Pro Enhanced" had been alluding to besides PSSR and ray-traced shadows.

I'd concede that part of the problem is my own PC-gaming-oriented setup, which makes the flaws impossible to overlook. My Alienware AW2726DM is a QD-OLED, and since OLED pixels switch almost instantly, nothing blurs one frame into the next. At 30fps, every quick swing of the camera turns into a series of visible steps, so it was almost inevitable that I'd reach for a workaround sooner rather than later.

GTA 6's Xbox executable has leaked, opening the door for unofficial PC port projects to start testing

Cyberleek followed through and leaked the missing file required to get PC porting efforts underway.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

All I needed was a feed of GTA 6 on my PC

An open-source app beat Sony to it

These days, all that one often needs for frame generation to work is a feed of the game. My first mistake was assuming that Sony's official Remote Play app would be the best way to get it. Much to my surprise, the app crashed every time I opened it, and every troubleshooting effort went absolutely nowhere.

So I took the path of least resistance: using chiaki-ng. It's a free, open-source Remote Play client that talks to the PS5 using the same protocol as Sony's app. Once it was paired, it took me a few minutes and some fine-tuning related to the DualSense to get GTA 6 up and running on my PC in Windows 11.

Immediately after the first boot, I reached for Lossless Scaling, a $7 frame generation and upscaling app on Steam. Remote Play caps the output at 1080p, so chiaki-ng's built-in upscaler upscaled the stream to match the monitor's 1440p, and Lossless Scaling generated frames on top of it.

This, however, created two problems: latency and interpolation artifacts, both by-products of frame generation. The artifacts flared up on Jason's face on fast camera swings, and on top of that, Lossless Scaling's FSR pass made everything grainy and stole from the visuals, which, in a game that looks this good, was an unacceptable compromise.

The latency was the bigger issue here. Lossless Scaling can't build an in-between frame until the next real frame arrives, and at 30fps, the next one is always 33.3ms away. That made sudden movements unplayable, and when driving in a game that's as fast-paced as GTA 6, not registering those movements in time is the best way to drive head-first into the oncoming traffic.

SmoovPlay got the lag out of the way

And RTX Video Super Resolution got rid of the grain

At this point, my experiments with Lossless Scaling coupled with chiaki-ng had replaced one compromise with another, so the next step was finding a way to address latency as much as possible and the graininess imparted by FSR. The solution to both problems for me came through SmoovPlay, another free, open-source tool with the Remote Play client built in. It worked better because it could generate frames straight from the video stream instead of capturing a window on my screen.

The frame generation on SmoovPlay comes from RIFE, an AI interpolation model, and for upscaling, it offers a choice between FSR 1 and Nvidia's RTX Video Super Resolution. On my RTX 4070 Ti Super, I went with the latter, and the graininess that FSR had left all over the stream in my first setup was gone.

As I got behind the wheel, the difference almost felt like magic. Input delay felt absent, and driving with precision was finally possible. Streetlights and crosswalks stayed sharp, and the unpleasant smearing around the car was gone too. SmoovPlay's counter put its added delay at 18ms, though that figure only covered its own processing, not the full trip from my analog stick to the screen, so I'd take it with a grain of salt.

I didn't need a capture card to play GTA 6 at 60fps

For anyone excited about the SmoovPlay approach, one thing to note is that GTA 6 still responds to input 30 times per second, and every extra frame is generated on my PC. SmoovPlay, in my experience, hides the seams better than everything else I've tried, and without a capture card, it's the one approach worth taking.

item.title: The Garmin Vivoactive 5 is tied with its all-time low at $152
item.itunes:title: The Garmin Vivoactive 5 is tied with its all-time low at $152
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Smartwatch prices rarely dip this low for a brand as reputable as Garmin, but the vívoactive 5 is currently sitting at its all-time low on Amazon. The 42mm Orchid model has dropped from its regular $299.99 price tag to just $152.09, a savings of $147.90 that makes this one of the most compelling deals right now.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Garmin Vivoactive 5

The Garmin Vivoactive 5 is perfect for those who are looking to buy a reliable Garmin activity tracker without spending too much money. Not only is it a bit on the affordable side, but it's also not nearly as bulky as other Garmin devices out there, making it suitable for more users.

See at Amazon

Why the Garmin vívoactive 5 is worth the discount

Garmin is known for building durable, long-lasting devices that prioritize health data over flashy features, and the vívoactive 5 is a prime example of that philosophy. It sits below the premium Forerunner and Fenix lines but offers a far more robust experience than most budget options.

If you are looking for a reliable companion for daily workouts, sleep tracking, or general health monitoring without breaking the bank, this is the moment to strike. The core of the vívoactive 5 is its health monitoring suite, which is extensive even at this price point.

It features 24/7 heart rate monitoring, stress tracking, and the Body Battery energy monitoring system that helps you understand when your body is charged up and when it needs rest. This isn't just a step counter; it's a comprehensive health coach that integrates with the Garmin Connect app to provide personalized insights based on your sleep, naps, and workout intensity.

One of the standout features for active users is the inclusion of over 30 built-in sports apps. Whether you are into running, cycling, swimming, or HIIT, the watch has a dedicated mode for it. It also supports wheelchair mode, which tracks pushes rather than steps, making it a more inclusive option for many users.

The watch also offers automatic nap detection, allowing it to log your rest throughout the day and show how it impacts your overall energy levels. For those who prefer not to carry their phone on runs, the vívoactive 5 has enough storage to hold music playlists from Spotify, Amazon Music, or Deezer, and it supports wireless headphones for phone-free listening.

Battery life is another area where Garmin excels. The vívoactive 5 is rated for up to 11 days in smartwatch mode, which is significantly longer than most competitors in this price range. This means you can go a week or more without thinking about a charger, a huge benefit for travel or busy weeks.

The display is a bright, colorful 1.2-inch AMOLED screen with a resolution of 390 x 390, offering excellent visibility even in direct sunlight. The case is made of fiber-reinforced polymer and the band is silicone, both of which are durable and easy to clean. The watch is also water-resistant to 50 meters, so it is safe for swimming and showering.

This is a great model to own and at one of its best prices. Get it now before it's gone. You don't need to wait until Black Friday to shop.

item.title: Swapping my Pi pile for a 3D printed rack changed how my whole home lab looks
item.itunes:title: Swapping my Pi pile for a 3D printed rack changed how my whole home lab looks
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My first home server was born from my old PC many years ago. Since then, I’ve always had at least one server at home. As the years went by, these machines shrank until I was able to run my home services on single-board computers like Raspberry Pis. But the Pi cases I bought were single, standalone cases. They were hard to organize, especially with drives hanging out of them, and my server table in my basement looked messy.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

When I found the PiRack, I knew my problems would be solved. Here was an expandable rack system for Raspberry Pis that would help keep my Pi servers manageable. I could keep them all in one place, and there were even bays to store drives, which was exactly what I needed.

Printing the PiRack

You can make it as high as you want

The PiRack consists of flat panels that fit together with vertical rails. These rails have slots for Pi bays, which are like drawers that slide into the slots. When the panels are put together with the rails, they form a vertical structure for various bays to slide into, where you can store servers and disks.

First, decide what you’ll store in your PiRack. For my first one, I knew I had two servers and two drives. That meant four bays. Unfortunately, the PiRack only comes with rails that support up to three bays, but others have created remixes that make the system more expandable.

One of these is PiRack Rails 4x, which is exactly what I needed. If you plan to expand further, there’s also a Stackable Base you can insert on top of a set of rails and then continue vertically with a new set. This makes it possible to expand as high as you want, while also giving the rack itself more strength.

Of course, you can’t expand the system too high unless you anchor it to something, or it’ll topple over. So plan carefully: decide what you need to store before you print.

Next, choose your bays. There are bays for Pi 0s, Pi 3s, Pi 4s, bays with screens, bays without screens, bays for SSDs, and more. There are even two different bays just for holding power supplies. Check out the remixes on the original design to see what’s out there.

Now you’re ready to print. Any filament works well; my PiRacks are regular old PLA. And you don’t need a lot of detail for these: .28mm layer height is fine. You might decide on a color scheme based on the function of your servers. I chose orange rails and black panels for my Syncthing/file servers, and I chose blue rails and black panels for my Nextcloud server.

First, print a top panel and a bottom panel. If you’re going high, print as many stackable bases as you need. Then print your rails. For rails, I recommend a higher infill, for reasons you’ll see later. Use 50% or higher if you can spare the filament.

Finally, print your bays. The bay rails on the sides that fit in the slots on the vertical rails should have support. The most efficient way to print this is to enable support in your slicer. I prefer tree supports, as they break off more easily than traditional supports.

7 Raspberry Pi cases you can 3D print in just a few hours

Discover the ultimate 3D-printed case for your Raspberry Pi project, then 3D print one yourself

By  Jeff Butts

Assembling the PiRack

Tolerances are tight; try not to break it

The first thing you’ll likely notice is how tight the rails are in comparison to the tabs/holes they’re supposed to fit into. To assemble the panels and the rails, you may need to tap on them gently with a rubber mallet to get them connected. This is why I recommended you make the rails stronger by adding infill. I’ve broken rails and had to re-print them because I hammered them in too hard.

If they’re too tight, and you’re afraid of breaking them, you’ll have to use a deburring tool on the holes to widen them a bit. If you do break tabs off, all is not lost: a drop of superglue stands in well for connecting panels to rails.

Be careful to make sure the rail slots are lined up, so they can accept your bays. Take your bays and slide them in, making sure they fit well. Sometimes they’re a little snug; a little household oil lubricates them nicely.

item.title: I used Cline with a local Qwen coding model in VS Code, and it handled most of what I paid Cursor for
item.itunes:title: I used Cline with a local Qwen coding model in VS Code, and it handled most of what I paid Cursor for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using AI coding tools like Cursor and Claude Code for quite some time now, and they've made it much easier to build personal projects without writing every line of code myself. Cursor, in particular, has been one of my go-to tools because of how well it integrates AI into the development environment. However, paying for another AI subscription isn't particularly appealing, especially since I already have several.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've also been experimenting with local LLMs, and I wanted to see if I could get a similar coding experience without relying on cloud models. So I installed Cline in VS Code, connected it to Qwen3.5-9B running locally through LM Studio, and put it to work. I used the setup to build an expense tracker and a task manager with its own API and frontend. To my surprise, this combination handled a significant portion of what I normally use Cursor for.

Cline brings Cursor-like features to VS Code

All you need is a capable local model

One of the biggest reasons I use Cursor is its ability to work on an entire project instead of simply generating snippets of code. You can ask it to add a feature, fix a bug, or make changes across multiple files, and its agent can inspect your codebase, execute terminal commands, and make the necessary modifications. Cline brings much of this functionality to regular VS Code, and it's completely free to install.

Cline is an open-source AI coding agent that supports several cloud and local models. It can read and modify files, run commands, identify errors, and work through development tasks with relatively little intervention. It also supports checkpoints, so you can restore previous versions of your files if the agent makes unwanted changes. The experience is similar to working with Cursor's Agent, although the quality of the results depends heavily on the model you connect.

For my setup, I used Qwen3.5-9B, a relatively small model that supports coding and tool calling. I already had LM Studio installed on my MacBook, so getting everything running didn’t take much time. I loaded the model in LM Studio, enabled its local API server, and selected LM Studio as the provider in Cline's settings.

I spent a month coding without VS Code, and I don't want to go back

Turns out, I wasn’t missing much

8
By  Parth Shah

I built two applications using a local 9B model

Putting Cline through real development tasks

I wanted to test the setup with something more substantial than generating a few functions or writing a simple Python script. For my first project, I asked Cline to build an expense tracker that would let me record transactions, categorize expenses, and keep track of my spending.

Cline approached the development process in the same way as Cursor. I could give it instructions and let it work directly on the project. It could create the necessary files, modify existing code, and use terminal commands as part of the development process. I could also inspect the changes and provide additional instructions whenever something needed adjusting.

For my second project, I made things a little more challenging by building a task manager with a separate API and frontend. The model had to create backend endpoints to manage tasks, build an interface to interact with them, and connect the two components. It's a more demanding exercise for a local model because changes to the backend need to be reflected correctly in the frontend.

I'm not going to lie, the model did struggle a lot to get things right, and I had to keep correcting it again and again. It definitely took a lot more for me to make the model get it right than what I would usually do with something like Claude.

I don't need Cursor for every coding project anymore

Local coding agents have become genuinely useful

I'm not going to pretend that Qwen3.5-9B can compete with the likes of Claude Sonnet or other frontier coding models. There is a very big difference in their ability to understand complicated instructions, reason through problems, and handle larger projects. A local model also has to work within the limitations of your hardware, which affects how quickly it generates responses and how much context it can process.

However, you don't necessarily need that level of intelligence for every coding task. A lot of my personal projects involve building small applications, adding features, fixing bugs, and experimenting with ideas. These are precisely the kinds of tasks where having an agent that can work directly with your files is useful. Even if Qwen requires more guidance than a larger cloud model, I can still get meaningful work done without consuming paid API credits.

There are also some things I would miss from Cursor. Its Tab autocomplete is particularly useful when you're writing code manually, and its integration with cloud models makes it more convenient for demanding projects. Cline doesn't offer the same autocomplete experience, and working with a smaller local model requires more patience, especially when a task involves several rounds of reasoning and tool execution.

I’d still keep using a local model

For me, the biggest advantage is being able to experiment without worrying about usage limits. I can ask Cline to try a different implementation, make changes to an existing project, or work through a problem without thinking about how many requests I've used. I still see plenty of reasons to keep a cloud coding agent around, particularly for complicated development work. But for smaller personal projects, Cline and a capable local model have made paying for another coding subscription a lot harder to justify.

I found a free Claude Code and Codex alternative that does almost everything I need for my work

Spinning hard drives down to standby saves a modest amount of wattage, but short idle timeouts combined with frequent background NAS tasks (such as indexing, S.M.A.R.T. polling, Docker/container logs, or array metadata checks) can trigger repeated start-stop and head load/unload cycles.

Spin-downs don't automatically kill every drive, but start-stop cycles, firmware power management, and OS-level timers can contribute to hard drive wear, and a single practical adjustment (disabling aggressive spin-down or raising the standby/APM threshold to match actual access patterns) can cut unnecessary cycling. We've had drives spin down while idle, but there are cases where you probably should consider otherwise or at least tune it so it won't prematurely kill your drives.

You may be causing unecessary wear and tear to your network storage.

By  Rich Edmonds

What is spin-down?

How does spinning down affect your drive health?

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

In order to understand how a spin-down can affect your hardware, you first have to understand the difference between a full spin-down and head load/unload cycles. A full spin down is when a device enters standby/sleep mode and the spindle rotation stops. Power drops to roughly 1W per drive. Head load/unload cycles are slightly different. This occurs when drives are moving read/write heads onto the ramp while platters continue spinning. It's easy to conflate the two, but both behave very differently under firmware and OS control.

Many modern hard drives carry rated load/unload cycle figures, often cited around 300,000 to 600,000 cycles, and start/stop readings, commonly around 50,000 cycles, under rated conditions. This depends on the drive specifications, but hitting this number doesn't spell failure, nor does spinning 24/7 eliminate wear. Rapid repeated start-stop cycling can add recurring mechanical and thermal transients.

It might be easy to think that spinning down your drives gives you free power savings, but this is often overestimated. A spinning idle drive may draw around 3W to 7W depending on model and RPM, while standby drops closer to 1W. Over a 24-hour day, saving a few watts per drive can yield fairly modest annual kWh reductions, which can be very small compared to the cost of a single premature replacement drive or the convenience cost of spin-up lag.

Your NAS might be fighting your drives

OS timers might hurt your drive health

Background noise of your NAS can wake up sleeping drives. In a live NAS environment, background services like file indexes, thumbnail generators, S.M.A.R.T health checks, container/VM writes, or even network discovery can touch a disk shortly after it enters standby. This means that your NAS software could be fighting with your drive's firmware. If the spin-down timer is set too low (for example, 5 to 15 minutes), the drive can cycle down and spin back up repeatedly throughout the day, creating wear.

OS standby timers also play a part. On Linux-based NAS setups, tools like hdparm interact with drive-level power modes, and sometimes drives ignore or override those timers depending on firmware and SATA/HBA behavior. Similarly, vendor power balance or head parking features can behave unexpectedly if left mismatched with your OS settings.

Array layouts can affect spin-down behavior pretty dramatically too. In some multi-disc pools or parity/striped arrays, waking one member disk or reading across stripes often requires multiple drives to spin up together, magnifying wake latency and power spikes across the entire enclosure.

You can verify what is happening in your own NAS by checking S.M.A.R.T. statistics before and after a 24-hour window, auditing which processes or shares wake disks, and spotting mismatches between NAS UI timers and actual disk power states. The most relevant counters to check are Start_Stop_Count (4) and, when supported by the drive, Load_Cycle_Count (193); Power_Cycle_Count (12) can be useful, but it tracks full power cycles, not routine spin-downs.

How to fix constant spin-down

One setting can make a major difference

The easiest fix is that, instead of chasing aggressive 5- or 10-minute spin-down timers, either disable automatic spin-down on actively used NAS drives (which will keep them spinning and essentially disable standby) or you can set a long standby window, such as several hours or overnight only, paired with proper APM/power settings, so drives aren't yo-yoing all day.

The exact commands and UI labels vary by OS, whether you're using TrueNAS, Unraid, OpenMediaVault, or even custom Linux. Be sure to double-check your vendor utilities where applicable, so you know what settings to adjust specifically. Some apps (Plex, Jellyfin, etc.) and OS will actually prevent drives from stopping altogether.

There are some instances where spin-down does make sense. For example, if you have cold/archive backup drives that are accessed only once a day or less, or fanless/quiet desktop enclosures where acoustics and heat matter, then spinning down your drives might make more sense. If you're in a high-electricity-rate area where idle wattage adds up, spinning down your drives might save you money in the long term.

No single power tweak will replace real reliability hygiene, so make sure that you keep your drive temperatures reasonable, run regular SMART short/long tasks, maintain parity/redundancy, and follow a 3-2-1 backup strategy so that your data is protected.

Don't let spin-down affect your drive health

Aggressive NAS spin-down schedules often trade measurable daily convenience and extra start-stop cycling for surprisingly small energy savings while in turn creating mechanical wear on your drive. It might be worth checking your own SMART counters, testing a longer spin-down interval, or keeping your active NAS drive spinning during heavy-use hours to measure the real power and wake behavior rather than relying on default timers.

item.title: Windows has had a built-in way to turn a drawer of mismatched old drives into one big pool for over a decade, and almost nobody uses it
item.itunes:title: Windows has had a built-in way to turn a drawer of mismatched old drives into one big pool for over a decade, and almost nobody uses it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's becoming exceedingly common for people, not just PC enthusiasts, to have spare storage lying around. It could be a 1TB drive from an old build or a 500GB SSD that's sitting in a PC nobody uses, and it's possible none of them are worth taking out to install on their own, so they continue to sit there.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Windows has had a solution for this since Windows 8, and it's gone largely unused by the majority of people with spare storage kicking about. It's called Storage Spaces, and it can take those mismatched drives and turn them into a single pool with one drive letter. It can protect you if one of them dies, and comes with Windows Home, so anyone can use it.

How I use software RAID on Windows to speed up drive access and add redundancy

Storage Spaces on Windows enables a simpler version of software RAID

By  Tanveer Singh

Storage Spaces is the new spanned volume replacement

Windows is pushing users to use these instead

If you've ever tried to combine the capacity of two drives into one in Windows using only a GUI, you've probably tried Disk Management's spanned volumes function. This approach relies on dynamic disks, which have largely been deprecated for everything besides boot volumes that are mirrored. Thus, the replacement is Storage Spaces, and to Microsoft's credit, it's better in so many ways.

Storage Spaces works by grouping two or more physical drives into a storage pool that is then carved into virtual drives, called storage spaces. Windows formats these virtual drives as if they're any other drive. In the background, Windows splits data saved to these spaces into 256MB chunks that are then spread across the drives in the pool. This is why capacity doesn't matter, and if you run low on space in the pool later, you can always just add another drive instead of starting over.

The other key difference between Storage Spaces and spanned volumes is protection. A spanned volume strings drives together end-to-end, so losing one of them means you lose the entire volume. Storage spaces can keep two copies of everything on separate drives, so one failure doesn't mean the entire space dies. One of the primary use cases for Storage Spaces is repurposing old storage which may be susceptible to failures in the future, so having some kind of redundancy built-in is important.

4 reasons to use multiple partitions on a Windows PC

There are still good reasons in 2025 to use multiple partitions on a Windows PC.

7
By  Brian Burgess

Setting up a Storage Space

It's pretty simple

In Windows 11, Storage Spaces lives in Settings under System > Storage > Advanced storage settings. The older Control Panel version is still there if you search for it, and both do the same job. You need at least two drives besides the one Windows is installed on.

Before going any further, though, you should make sure the drives you want to use don't contain any data you need to back up. Windows will warn you that the drives contain files before you continue, but it doesn't hurt to check beforehand. The wizard will then allow you to name the storage space and resiliency type, which depends on how many drives you select.

Simple combines all the capacity with no protection at all, a two-way mirror keeps two copies of every file on different drives and survives one drive failure, and finally, a three-way mirror keeps three copies and needs at least five drives. Parity works much like a standard RAID 5 would: it trades some capacity for protection and needs at least three drives.

4 reasons I use Virtual Hard Disks instead of partitioning my storage

Using a Virtual Hard Disk instead of partitioning your main drives offers added flexibility and convenience to a wide range of use cases.

2
By  Andre Revilla

There are a few caveats to using Storage Spaces

Microsoft doesn't put these in the wizard

Possibly the biggest downside of using Storage Spaces is that when using any kind of parity, performance can suffer immensely. Every write you make to a space using parity means recalculating said parity, and when using it on a few hard drives, that can slow things to a crawl. You can somewhat remedy this by recreating the space in PowerShell with tuned column and interleave values, but the standard wizard for creating a Storage Space doesn't expose this, and it's also far more than the average person will want to deal with.

Using internal drives for a storage space is one thing, but if you want to use an external drive, Microsoft themselves say yours might not work. These drives show themselves as removable, so they aren't always recognized as eligible for use in a Storage Space. Microsoft also limits volume creation to NTFS on consumer versions of Windows, which also limits Storage Spaces to NTFS. This is somewhat disappointing considering that it seems like a prime opportunity to use their proprietary ReFS filesystem, which can detect corruption and repair it in a sort of ZFS-like manner.

Stop using RAID 0, even if it's just for the speed

The only thing RAID 0 speeds up is the loss of your data!

32
By  Ayush Pande

It's not perfect but it's a great way to get some use out of old drives

Storage Spaces is far from perfect, but it's one of the better ways to combine a set of old drives within Windows. It certainly doesn't replace a proper NAS, and it certainly doesn't perform as well as one when parity is used, but as a way to reuse some drives you have sitting in a drawer, it does exactly what it says on the tin.

This compact device creates a mesh network outside of Wi-Fi channels, freeing up wireless bandwidth for clients such as smartphones and laptops. The end result is a network that not only works, but is also fairly resilient to one of these devices going offline. Not bad for a central hub costing $30, right? Grab one now before Black Friday ends!

item.title: 27 years ago, you could buy a PlayStation emulator in stores, but Sony’s lawsuits killed it
item.itunes:title: 27 years ago, you could buy a PlayStation emulator in stores, but Sony’s lawsuits killed it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Modern game preservation has reached a wonderfully strange point today. We've got fans tearing apart old console games, rebuilding them for modern hardware, and sometimes making them look better in the process. We now treat these projects as impressive technical feats, but nearly three decades ago, someone was already doing something remarkably similar with PlayStation games.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

In 1999, Bleem! let you play PS1 games on a PC by dynamically translating their code to run on completely different hardware. The most interesting part, though, was that it was a commercially sold PlayStation emulator, and you could walk into a store and buy it. Bleem! has to be one of the most fascinating pieces of software in gaming history, and it's a shame that it attracted the wrong kind of attention from Sony, who really didn't like what it was doing.

Yes, you could actually buy a PlayStation emulator

Bleem! made PlayStation games look better on a PC

Recompilation can make old console games feel almost native on different hardware. Bleem! was doing something remarkably similar in spirit back in 1999, except instead of downloading a simple zip file from a GitHub repo, you could walk into a store and buy the emulator.

Created by programmer Randy Linden and entrepreneur David Herpolsheimer, Bleem! was released for Windows in April 1999.

It dynamically recompiled PlayStation code into x86 instructions, allowing PS1 games to run on PCs without Sony's hardware or software. Programmer Randy Linden says he wrote the emulator entirely in x86 assembly, including a runtime-optimizing recompiler.

Furthermore, instead of just making PS games playable, Bleem! could use a PC's 3D accelerator to render them at higher resolutions with filtered textures and other enhancements. People's late-'90s PCs were making some PlayStation games look considerably cleaner. The compatibility wasn't perfect, but the technical achievement alone was ridiculous for something that could run on a Pentium 166MHz with about 16MB of RAM.

And Bleem! wasn't some dodgy download passed around on IRC. The software was commercially distributed by Navarre and reached major retailers including CompUSA, Fry's, Electronics Boutique, Hastings, and Virgin Megastores. The retail version cost $29.99, turning PlayStation emulation into something you could quite literally pick up alongside your other PC games.

Bleem! effectively (and single-handedly) set out to prove that emulation itself could be a legitimate commercial product, and for the most part, succeeded. That achievement, though, was rather short-lived, since Sony was about to take a very expensive interest in that idea.

Emulators save games that publishers have abandoned, but the industry still treats them like piracy

Game preservation often skirts the line between the legal and illegal

By  Tanveer Singh

Sony took Bleem! to court almost immediately

The emulator survived the lawsuits, but not the cost of fighting them

It's not hard to see that Sony wasn't particularly amused by the idea of people buying software that could turn a PC into a better-looking PlayStation. It sued Bleem! in April 1999, before the emulator's full commercial release, arguing that the company was infringing Sony's intellectual property.

Sony's problem, however, was that Bleem! had done absolutely nothing wrong, and the software had been deliberately designed to avoid the obvious legal tripwires. Bleem! didn't ship Sony's BIOS, PlayStation games, or Sony's copyrighted code. Its developers had reverse-engineered the console's behavior and written their own software to reproduce it.

For quite a while, Sony struggled to prove that Bleem! itself was actually infringing something Sony actually owned. The courts repeatedly declined to simply shut Bleem! down, allowing the emulator to remain on sale while the legal fight continued. Bleem! even turned the tables by countersuing Sony, arguing that Sony's campaign was harming its business.

That sounds like a victory, but winning in court and surviving in business are two very different things. Bleem! was a tiny company taking on one of the world's biggest gaming corporations, and every legal victory still meant another bill from its lawyers. Effectively speaking, Sony never proved that Bleem! was illegal. However, Sony still managed to make the emulator disappear by making it impossibly expensive to defend.

Bleem! also went after the Dreamcast

Bleemcast! turned Sega's console into an unlikely PlayStation

  • Credit: Ryan Somma / Flickr
  • Credit: Sergiy Galyonkin / Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr - Yoppy
  • Credit: Bryan Ochalla / Flickr
  • Credit: Adam Dachis / Flickr
  • Credit: Ryan Somma / Flickr
  • Credit: Sergiy Galyonkin / Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr - Yoppy
  • Credit: Bryan Ochalla / Flickr

Bleem! wasn't content with bringing PlayStation games to PCs. It eventually set its sights on Sega's Dreamcast, whose considerably more powerful hardware made it an excellent target for running enhanced PS1 games. The result was Bleemcast!, a heavily optimized version of the emulator designed specifically for Sega's console. And yes, you could actually buy that too.

The Dreamcast's hardware gave Bleem! considerably more headroom than the original PlayStation, allowing games to look dramatically cleaner while retaining the original software. The idea was to put a PlayStation disc into a Dreamcast, boot Bleemcast!, and play the game with higher-resolution visuals and improved texture filtering.

Sadly, that idea never came to full fruition, since Sega decided to part ways with the Bleem! team. Thankfully, even Microsoft showed interest in the project, according to Randy Linden. Linden has said Microsoft wanted to know whether Bleem's technology could help bring PlayStation games to the hardware that would eventually become the original Xbox, and that Bleem! received an offer from Microsoft that it ultimately rejected.

But Bleem! never got the chance to turn that interest into another business. Only a handful of Bleemcast! titles reached consumers before the company's finances collapsed. Even though Bleem! survived Sony's courtroom assault, it were running out of money, and that was the biggest problem.

Someone built a gadget that lets the Dreamcast play N64 games, and it's absolutely wild

The Dreamcart can also play SNES and Sega Genesis cartridges.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Bleem! won the fight but lost the war

Sony didn't have to beat it in court to take it off the shelves

Credit: Mayuki Sawatari via Wikimedia Commons

The irony of Bleem!'s downfall is that Sony never needed a decisive courtroom victory. Bleem! had spent millions defending itself, with one account putting legal fees at roughly a quarter of Bleem!'s $5.4 million in sales.

In fact, Bleem! even alleged that Sony pressured retailers by threatening their PS2 allocations if they carried its products, although that remained an allegation rather than a court finding. By November 2001, Bleem! was finished, and its equipment was eventually auctioned off on eBay.

The Dreamcast's collapse only made things worse. Sega discontinued the console in March 2001, removing the platform Bleemcast! was supposed to exploit just as Bleem! was fighting for survival. The company's shutdown page reportedly showed Sonic holding a flower beside a Bleem! gravestone, which is an almost comically bleak way to end a software company.

And yet, Bleem! left behind something far more valuable than what you might find in sales figures. Its technology proved that sophisticated console software could be translated to entirely different hardware without simply copying the original code. In one final twist, programmer Randy Linden himself later went to work at Sony. The company that fought his emulator eventually became part of his career in PlayStation technology.

I stopped using 4K upscaling for emulation, and my childhood games finally looked right

Nothing quite like native retro resolution with the right effect

6
By  Samarveer Singh

The recompiler that arrived decades too early

For anyone interested in game preservation, Bleem! is impossible not to admire. It arrived before the technology, business models, and legal expectations around preserving old games had settled into anything resembling normality.

That makes Bleem! feel less like an obscure footnote and more like an early warning. The technical barriers that once made old games prisoners of their original consoles have steadily fallen, but the uncomfortable questions around ownership haven't disappeared. If anything, modern recompilations are proving just how much life remains in software whose creators stopped supporting it decades ago. Bleem! simply figured that out first.

The Dreamcast's collapse only made things worse. Sega discontinued the console in March 2001, removing the platform Bleemcast! was supposed to exploit just as Bleem! was fighting for survival. The company's shutdown page reportedly showed Sonic holding a flower beside a Bleem! gravestone, which is an almost comically bleak way to end a software company.

And yet, Bleem! left behind something far more valuable than what you might find in sales figures. Its technology proved that sophisticated console software could be translated to entirely different hardware without simply copying the original code. In one final twist, programmer Randy Linden himself later went to work at Sony. The company that fought his emulator eventually became part of his career in PlayStation technology.

Nothing quite like native retro resolution with the right effect

The recompiler that arrived decades too early

For anyone interested in game preservation, Bleem! is impossible not to admire. It arrived before the technology, business models, and legal expectations around preserving old games had settled into anything resembling normality.

That makes Bleem! feel less like an obscure footnote and more like an early warning. The technical barriers that once made old games prisoners of their original consoles have steadily fallen, but the uncomfortable questions around ownership haven't disappeared. If anything, modern recompilations are proving just how much life remains in software whose creators stopped supporting it decades ago. Bleem! simply figured that out first.

item.itunes:title: This NAS lets you upgrade more than drives and I'm all for it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Not everyone wants to build their own home NAS, which means looking at prebuilt enclosures. However, even the best NAS devices offer little upgradability once you've picked a box. You can usually upgrade RAM and storage, and maybe add in PCIe cards for networking or caching, but that's it.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Not every company is working to that set of design restrictions. I've long used a Beelink ME mini as an all-flash NAS, so I was excited when they asked if I wanted to take a look as the new Beelink ME Pro. This metal NAS comes in 2- and 4-bay options, and a wide array of CPU, RAM, and SSD options. What's more, those options don't disappear after your initial choice, since the motherboard is designed as a module you can swap out. Current options include a range of Intel and AMD CPUs, but Arm-based modules are on the way too. In a sea of boring black boxes, it's a shining example of what can happen if you go against the norm.

About this review: Beelink provided the NAS unit used in this review. The company had no input into its contents, nor did it see it before publication.

Beelink ME Pro
Brand
Beelink
CPU
Intel Pentium Silver J5005 (4C/4T), Intel N95 (4C/4T), Intel N150 (4C/4T), Intel Core 3 304 (5C/5T), Intel Core i5-13500H (12C/16T), AMD Ryzen AI 7 H 350 (8C/16T), AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 (12C/24T)

Caching
Up to two M.2 SSD ports (can also be used for storage pool if not for cache)

The Beelink ME Pro is a powerful NAS unit with a unique selling point: the motherboard is modular so you can upgrade it in the future or swap between Intel, AMD (and upcoming Qualcomm) options.

Pros & Cons
  • Beautiful aluminum enclosure
  • Interchangeable motherboards
  • Plenty of connectivity
  • More powerful CPU options are expensive
  • Only the AMD versions are good for AI use
$819 at Kickstarter

Price, specs, and availability of the Beelink ME Pro

The Beelink ME Pro is currently only available on Kickstarter, where it has a couple of weeks left on the clock. I'm pretty sure it'll be available from Beelink and Amazon, etc., at the beginning of 2027, but if you want it early with a nice discount, it's time to head to the crowdfunding site.

It currently starts at $299 for a J5005 CPU and 2 bays, up to a 4-bay Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 at $1,379. These are crowdfunding prices, and the retail MSRP will be about 30% higher. Our review unit has an Intel i5-13500H and costs $819 right now.

What I liked about the Beelink ME Pro

This is a powerful NAS

The 4- and 2-bay units differ only in the number of drive bays, so assume everything I talk about applies to either. The ME Pro has one feature I haven't seen before: a replaceable motherboard module that is essentially a mini PC on a tray. It's the same module for either bay configuration, and you can buy the options separately.

The modules differ slightly in features, depending on the CPU they use. Our review unit with an Intel i5-13500H has a Thunderbolt 4 port, two M.2 slots for caching or storage pools, and two more M.2 slots under the blower-style heatsink. One of those has a 512GB SSD with FygoOS installed. You can get to that SSD and swap it for a larger one, but the slots under the blower aren't as fast as the others, so it's best used for the OS anyway. It also means you can upgrade it if you want to run another OS, like Proxmox or TrueNAS, or use it for caching.

You also get SODIMM RAM slots so you can upgrade them. Again, our review unit has 32GB of DDR4 and can be upgraded up to 96GB, although current prices make that prohibitively expensive.
